newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-BASF profits up, eyes stronger growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BASF profits up, eyes stronger growth.

text.p: German chemicals group BASF AG said on Wednesday group pre-tax profit rose 8.8 percent in the first nine months of 1996 and painted a slightly rosier picture for future growth.

Highlighting improved business conditions in the third quarter BASF said three months sales to September 30 climbed 7.2 percent to 11.9 billion marks ($7.9 billion) while nine-month sales rose 2.9 percent to 36.1 billion marks.
Pre-tax profits in the first nine months of the year totalled 3.4 billion marks but showed a 2.3 percent drop to 1.04 billion marks in the third quarter.
Like its German rivals, BASF suffered from a three percent drop in prices but said a 3.7 percent increase in volume sales largely offset weaker prices.

BASF said favourable currency movements, particularly the mark's weakness against the dollar, which made german exports cheaper abroad, contributed a 1.6 percent increase to growth. Last year the company had grappled with the negative effects of a strong mark.
Strong third quarter results and signs that prices were beginning to pick up again in certain sectors left BASF chief executive Juergen Strube confident the recovery would continue.
"Despite one-time costs, we expect the 1996 result to be near year ago levels," Strube said, adding the recovery should also continue into the first months of 1997.

But true to his conservative style, Strube declined to be drawn further, saying only, "I am very cautious about using the word record (when discussing future results)...we are in November and as you know things often happen before year end."
Last year BASF posted a pre-tax profit of 4.13 billion marks with sales at 46.2 billion marks and a return on assets before taxes and interest expenses at 11.2 percent.

Analysts said Strube's reserved outlook was partly responsible for the share's weakness in Frankfurt bourse trading. BASF shares ended floor dealings up 21 pfennigs at 51.55, weaker than the rest of the market, which was at record high levels.
But Strube hinted the group may announce a higher dividend by saying BASF's shareholders may have reason to celebrate the payout after receiving a 14 mark dividend in 1995, up from 10 marks for 1994.

To fuel future growth BASF continues to eye acquisitions and possible divestments, Strube said, after the company sold its tape business BASF Magnetics GmbH and is confident of completing the sale of a 51 percent stake in Kali und Salz Beteiligungs AG to Canada's Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan this year.
Among its various businesses, health and nutrition posted an 18.4 percent jump to 7.1 billion marks in the first nine months. Oil and Gas sales jumped 12.4 percent to 3.5 billion marks.

BASF is particularly optimistic for its health business saying the acquisition of the drugs business of U.S. Boots had already fuelled growth and a planned takeover of Sandoz AG's maize herbicide business should further support growth.

Focusing on the development of innovative drugs, BASF hopes to post drug sales of four to five billion marks a year by the year 2000 as new products, including obesity drug Meridia, strengthen the product palette. 1996 drug sales will be near 3.4 billion marks.

Analysts say BASF may now be ready to again search for a target in the drugs sector after having successfully digested the Boots acquisition. Strube only said BASF wanted to seize appropriate opportunities in a consolidating industry.

In the first nine months, sales in Latin America measured the strongest increase of 26.3 percent with Europe, BASF's single largest market, showed a 0.7 percent drop in sales to 22.5 billion marks in the first nine months.

Strube however stressed BASF's commitment to the European market, the world's largest chemical market, saying, "We want to participate in the opportunities of the European market and thus plan to further strengthen our position here."

The strong focus on Europe appears to contrast with an earlier and highly publicised interest in Asia and criticism about high business costs in Germany. Strube countered that interest in the Asian and American growth regions remained but that Europe would continue to reign as the world's biggest market for another 15 years at least.
